extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists and activists interested in media freedom and censorship in Thailand
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of laws, institutions, practices, and examples of media censorship in Thailand across print, broadcast, film, radio, and the internet. Covers constitutional text, statutes, administrative practice, and notable incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional guarantees of freedom of communication and expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections of the 2007 Constitution (e.g., Section 36, Section 45) guarantee liberty of communication and the liberty to express opinions, make speeches, write, print, publicize, and make expression by other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional text quoted: 'A person shall enjoy the liberty of communication by any means...'; 'A person shall enjoy the liberty to express his or her opinion, make speeches, write, print, publicize, and make expression by other means.' These are presented as formal guarantees framing media law and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted restrictions on constitutional rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions on communication and expression are permitted only 'by virtue of the provisions of the law specifically enacted for security of the state or maintaining public order or good morals' and to safeguard rights, dignity, reputation, family or privacy, or prevent deterioration of public mind or health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional provisos require restrictions to be enacted by law and 'shall not affect the essential substances' of such rights (Section 29). This language functions as a legal standard used to justify censorship actions in practice (security/public order/good morals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of prior official censorship except during war or armed conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution states 'Censorship by a competent official of news and articles before their publication in a newspaper, printed matter, or radio or television broadcasting shall not be made except during the time when the country is in a state of war or armed conflict'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constitutional rule is a formal limit on prior restraint, but the article documents many forms of de facto pre-publication control (e.g., film board cuts, broadcasters' self-censorship) that circumvent or operate alongside it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media ownership and subsidy restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution provides that the owner of a newspaper or other mass media business shall be a Thai national and 'No grant of money or other properties shall be given by the state as subsidies to private newspapers or other mass media.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership and subsidy rules are regulatory constraints that shape who can own media and reduce state funding routes, but ownership rules also have been used politically (state influence via ownership or control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing and Advertisement Act enforcement powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the 1941 Printing and Advertisement Act, the Royal Thai Police Special Branch has authority to issue warnings to publications for violations such as 'disturbing the peace, interfering with public safety, or offending public morals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory power is cited as a ground for issuing warnings, removing material, and controlling print media content; historically used to ban books and periodicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lèse‑majesté (insulting the monarchy) as a censorship criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of the king is banned and lèse‑majesté laws are commonly used for censorship and political suppression in Thailand; enforcement has increased and been applied to journalists, bloggers, foreigners and citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents dramatic increases in lèse‑majesté prosecutions, online and offline cases, and how this law functions as a dominant legal basis for restricting political speech about the monarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation/libel laws used to suppress criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation and criminal libel laws have long been used to silence government critics, journalists, and commentators; libel suits have been filed against critics and media organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include high-profile suits (e.g., Thaksin-era cases), and the text notes the threat of libel suits encourages self-censorship and legal pressure on media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film Censorship Board rules and pre‑submission requirements (pre‑2008 practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Until 2008 the Film Censorship Board required theatre owners/broadcasters to submit films for review; the board (composed of multiple ministries and the military) could demand cuts or ban films if requirements were not met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board members cited 'sex and nudity' and failure to respect religion or national security as reasons for cuts or bans; submission and mandatory cuts constitute a formal pre-publication/regulatory control mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film censorship substantive criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons given for censoring films include 'violating moral and cultural norms and disturbing the public order and national security'; specific grounds include mentioning prostitution or failing to depict Buddhism with reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides examples (Schindler's List initial ban for nudity; films banned for unfavorable depictions of monks or monarchy) illustrating how these broad criteria are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion Pictures and Video Act rating system (post‑2008 reform)
rubrics_metrics.description: With the Motion Pictures and Video Act B.E. 2551 (2008) Thailand introduced a motion picture ratings system (13+, 15+, 18+, 20+) implemented in 2009, alongside a still‑existing Board of Censors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes industry hopes that a formal rating system would allow more viewer choice and reduce mandatory cuts, though the Board's powers remained a concern in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television content censorship practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Television broadcasts censor scenes such as 'clothes showing cleavage, a man's bare chest, weapons pointed at people, consumption of alcohol and even the bottom of a shoe' (showing one's heel considered rude); criticism of the king is prohibited on TV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes blurring and cutting practices, and that blurs may be omitted when the same show is broadcast overseas; also documents military occupation and direct pressure on TV news after coups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio licensing and community broadcast restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio stations must be government licensed and have been primarily operated by government/military; the Broadcasting Act of 2008 authorizes community broadcast licenses for non‑commercial local service and prohibits community broadcasters from engaging in commercial activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government/military ownership and licensing regimes are described as structural constraints that undermine radio freedom; community radio expansion is noted alongside fears of political interference and limited issuance of licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet censorship authorities and mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet censorship is carried out by Royal Thai Police, the Communications Authority of Thailand, and the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology (now Ministry of Digital Economy and Society). Blocking is done by URL and/or IP address, by court order and informal requests to ISPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that MICT informally 'requests' ISPs to block sites and threatens sanctions (bandwidth restriction or loss of license) for non‑compliance, producing large-scale informal blocking beyond court orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories/reasons for internet blocking
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported blocking reasons include lèse‑majesté/national security/political issues, pornographic content, gambling, copyright infringement, illegal products and services, illegal drugs, sales of sex equipment, prostitution, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives percentages (e.g., growth in proportion of lèse‑majesté–related blocks after 2006) and notes tens of thousands of URLs blocked both by court order and informally under emergency decrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer Crime Act and cyber‑policing as grounds for prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Computer Crime Act and related cyber‑policing measures have contributed to increases in lèse‑majesté and other prosecutions; digital forensics and cooperation with universities are used to investigate online speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article links the Act to a sharp increase in cases tried each year and describes government expansion of digital forensic resources and interagency cooperation to support prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of emergency decrees and internal security laws to broaden censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency decrees, the Internal Security Act, and other extraordinary powers have been used to expand censorship beyond ordinary statutes, permitting informal blocking and restrictions during unrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include censorship growth after the 2006 coup, expanded focus from pornography to lèse‑majesté and political content, and blocking under emergency provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative pressure and informal limits on reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Military and government representatives have met with editors and journalists to set 'limits' on reporting, ask for 'constructive reporting', or request positive coverage; editors and hosts have been pressured, removed, or programs axed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include junta meetings with newspaper editors, threats to stations after coups, military orders to avoid interviewing academics who could 'incite conflict', and visits to Thai PBS to pressure programming decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign film/production permissions and content review
rubrics_metrics.description: All foreign companies must apply for shooting permission to the Film Board of Thailand; 'Some topics will be rejected if the script is judged inappropriate' and the Film Board 'checks to see that the script, plot, and other details are acceptable to the board.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a pre‑approval mechanism for foreign productions with explicit script/plot review and potential rejection on content grounds (e.g., material judged damaging to the country or monarchy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self‑censorship as an outcome of legal and extra‑legal pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Self‑censorship is a 'growing trend' in Thailand, driven largely by fear of lèse‑majesté, libel suits, and political/economic pressure; institutions such as bookstores and university outlets have refused to carry titles even when not officially banned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents examples (bookstores refusing works, media preemptively altering broadcasts) demonstrating how formal laws and informal pressures translate into avoidance of sensitive topics by authors, publishers, and broadcasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishments and criminal penalties as deterrents
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal penalties—such as jail sentences (the maximum for some offences noted as seven years)—are used for offences including criticism of court judgments and lèse‑majesté, creating strong deterrent effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites cases where individuals were jailed for political speech and notes the severe sentencing framework that contributes to chilling effects on speech.
